I want to be clear about how the fund will operate, because there has been some confusion. Bids will be led by local authorities, working with their Members of Parliament and with local business and community partners. We are deliberately keeping the application process simpler than the schemes it replaces, because we heard repeatedly that smaller councils with fewer staff were being outbid not on the merits of their projects but on the polish of their paperwork. Capacity funding will be made available so that those places can compete properly.

I also want to address the question of prioritisation, which several hon. Members have raised. The index we have published is based on need for economic recovery, on the opportunity for improved transport connectivity, and on the prevailing level of deprivation. It is not a ranking of who deserves money and who does not. Every place can bid, and every bid will be assessed on its own strength.

What matters ultimately is whether, in five or ten years, people in the towns we are talking about can point to something and say that it changed. A refurbished market hall. A reopened line. A safe route to school. That is the test I expect to be held to, and it is the right one.

That is what this legislation is about, at bottom. It is about whether the pathways we describe to our children in cheerful terms are actually walkable when they arrive. It is easy in this place to speak about labour market participation and skills pipelines as though they were plumbing diagrams. They are not. They are the accumulated choices of millions of families about what seems possible.

Local transport plans are, in my experience, excellent documents. They are well written, they cite the right evidence, and they set out sensible sequencing. What they cannot do is conjure capital. A combined authority can plan a segregated cycle network across three boroughs, but if the funding settlement arrives in one-year tranches with competitive bidding attached, what gets built is whatever can be designed and delivered inside twelve months. That is how we end up with disconnected fragments of cycle lane that stop at ward boundaries and are then held up as evidence that active travel does not work.

On buses, the position is more serious still. Since deregulation, mileage outside London has fallen substantially, and the commercial network has retreated to the routes that pay. Franchising offers a way out, but the process is long, legally contested, and expensive before a single additional service runs. I would like to hear from the Minister what support is available to authorities pursuing it, and whether the Department will underwrite the transition costs.

I also want to mention low carbon solutions specifically. Zero emission buses are welcome, and the orders placed have supported manufacturing jobs. But a zero emission bus that nobody catches because it runs twice a day is not a decarbonisation strategy. Frequency is the environmental policy. Reliability is the environmental policy.

My request is simple. Give the combined authority a multi-year settlement it can plan against, devolve the decisions about how it is spent, and then hold it accountable for outcomes rather than for process. That is the arrangement that works everywhere it has been tried.

I understand the concerns that have been raised about free expression, and I do not dismiss them. We should always be uneasy when a legislature decides that a particular statement may not be made. That unease is healthy. But we already accept limits in this area. We prohibit incitement, we prohibit the wilful promotion of hatred, and we do so because we recognise that some speech operates not as argument but as recruitment. Denial is of that kind. Its function is to tell the survivor that their memory is fraudulent and to tell the sympathiser that the crime was never so bad.

There is a second reason this matters now, and it goes to the point about survivors. For eighty years, denial in this country ran up against the immovable fact of people who were there. You could not tell a room that it did not happen when a woman in the third row could roll up her sleeve. That generation is leaving us. Within a very short time there will be no one who can answer from personal knowledge. The testimony remains, the archives remain, and the scholarship is overwhelming. But the living rebuttal will be gone, and those who wish to falsify the record know it. They have been waiting.

So the timing is not incidental to this measure. It is the reason for it. We are legislating at the moment when memory passes into history, and history, unlike memory, has no one to defend it but us.

Let me set out three things that I think require honesty. First, on capacity. The additional beds announced yesterday are welcome, but beds are not the binding constraint and everybody in this Chamber knows it. Staff are the binding constraint. You cannot recruit a specialist nurse in a fortnight, and the vacancies we are trying to fill now are the consequence of training decisions taken years ago. I would rather Ministers said that plainly than implied that money alone will solve it.

Second, on the supply chain. We have had a series of announcements about procurement, and I welcome the improvements in transparency. But we are still buying at the top of a global market from a standing start, and the premium we are paying is enormous. The question I want answered is what the domestic manufacturing plan is for the medium term, because the answer cannot be that we do this again next time.

Third, on public consent. This is the one I worry about most. People have complied to a remarkable degree, and they have done so largely on trust. Trust is depleted by rules that appear arbitrary, by guidance that changes on a Friday evening, and above all by the sense that the rules apply differently to different people. Once it goes, it does not come back quickly.

I say all of this as someone who wants the Government to succeed. There is no partisan advantage in failure here. But the reality check I mentioned has to include Ministers, and it has to start with an honest account of where we actually are.

Let me deal with the substance. The concern that has been put is that these provisions cut across obligations we have entered into. I do not accept the characterisation, but I understand why it is made, and it deserves a serious answer rather than a slogan. The position is this. The protocol was agreed on the basis that it would operate with the consent of both communities and that it would not disrupt the internal market of the United Kingdom. Both of those conditions are load-bearing. Where the practical operation of the arrangements begins to undermine them, we have not only a right but a duty to act.

On unfettered access specifically, I would remind the House what it means in practice. It means a manufacturer in Ballymena can sell to a customer in Birmingham without a customs declaration, without a rules-of-origin check, and without a delay at the port. Something like sixty per cent of Northern Ireland's external sales go to Great Britain. That is not a symbolic matter. It is the difference between a business being viable and not.

I recognise there are legitimate questions about how the arrangements interact with the single market, and about what checks are required in the other direction. We are engaged in detailed technical discussion on precisely those points, and I would ask the House to allow that discussion the space to produce something.

What I will not do is pretend to a certainty I do not have about timing. I have been asked repeatedly for a date. I would rather be criticised for vagueness now than for a broken promise later.

At the moment a driver may need four or five separate accounts, each with its own app, its own subscription, and its own tariff structure, simply to be confident of charging on a long journey. That is a straightforward equity problem. We are constructing a system in which the wealthier driver with a driveway pays a fraction of what the terraced-house driver pays for the same electricity. If we do not address the VAT differential and the standing charges built into public tariffs, we will entrench that.

On the grid itself, I would press the Minister on connection queues. I have spoken to operators with sites ready to go, planning permission secured, hardware ordered, waiting years for a connection date. That is not a market failure that the market will fix.

Finally, reliability. Every driver has a story about arriving at a charger that is broken, occupied by a petrol car, or requiring an app that will not load in an area with no signal. The people who signed this petition are not activists imported from elsewhere. They are commercial fishers who have watched their openings shrink year after year. They are members of first nations whose food fisheries have been closed. They are guides, lodge operators, and retired biologists who have been counting fish in the same creeks for thirty years and who can tell you, without consulting a chart, that the runs are not what they were. The science is not seriously in dispute on the direction of travel. Returns on several major systems have declined to a fraction of historical levels. Warming rivers, habitat loss from logging and development, and the cumulative effects of open net-pen operations along migration routes are all implicated. The disagreement is about weighting, and the weighting is exactly what an independent regulator would be able to assess without institutional pressure pulling in one direction.

Petitioners further call on the government to accelerate the transition to closed containment, with a firm date rather than a rolling review, and to fund habitat restoration at a scale commensurate with the problem rather than through small competitive grant rounds that consume more in application effort than they deliver.

I would add my own observation. Pacific salmon are not merely an industry. They are the nutrient pathway that feeds the forests, the basis of legal obligations to first nations that predate this Parliament, and a species around which entire coastal cultures are organized. We have managed them to the brink while producing a great many reports about managing them.

I am honoured to present this petition.

The point I would make to the House is that these excise reductions were introduced as an emergency response to a price shock, and they were always described as temporary. The difficulty, as every finance minister discovers, is that temporary reductions in fuel duty acquire a constituency very quickly.

I will set out the fiscal position honestly. The measures have cost the Exchequer a substantial sum, and each extension costs more. That money is not free. It comes either from borrowing, which we are trying to reduce, or from expenditure that would otherwise go to social protection, health, or the energy credits that are far better targeted at the households under genuine pressure. A cut in excise gives the largest absolute benefit to the person who buys the most fuel, which is not, on the whole, the person in greatest need.

That said, I accept the argument the Deputy has made about the haulage sector specifically. Hauliers cannot easily pass on costs in the short term because their contracts are fixed, they cannot substitute away from diesel because there is no alternative available at scale, and margins in the sector are genuinely thin. The rebate exists precisely because of that, and I am open to examining whether its thresholds remain appropriate given where prices have settled.

On the restoration of the rates, I have said before and I will repeat that it will be phased. A single-step restoration would produce exactly the kind of price jump at the pump that feeds back into headline inflation and into wage expectations. Phasing avoids that.

I would also note, because it is rarely mentioned, that carbon taxation and excise are doing different jobs, and the revenue from the former is hypothecated to retrofitting and to social protection measures. I do not intend to unravel that.

I want to draw out the general lesson, because it bears on the amendment before us. What worked during the pandemic was not centrally designed. It was local authorities and community organisations who already knew which streets had the highest concentration of shielding residents, which families were relying on free school meals, and which of the corner shops would deliver. They knew because they had been doing the work for years, in many cases with budgets that had been cut repeatedly. When the emergency came, we discovered that the infrastructure we had been steadily hollowing out was the infrastructure we needed.

The holiday hunger provision is the clearest example. For years the argument was made in this Chamber that feeding children during school holidays was not the state's business, that it would create dependency, that parents should manage. Then a footballer wrote a letter, and it turned out to be perfectly affordable after all. I make that point not to be gratuitous but because the speed of the reversal tells us something about how firmly the original position was actually held.

So my request to the Minister is about permanence. Emergency schemes have a way of being celebrated and then quietly discontinued once the emergency is declared over. The need did not begin in March 2020 and it has not ended. Child poverty in Cardiff, as across Wales, was rising before the pandemic and the drivers of it are structural: insecure work, housing costs, and a social security system with a two-child limit that no one in government will publicly defend on its merits.

I hope the Minister will address that directly.

I mention that because the debate about cash and the closure of bank branches is often framed as nostalgia, and I want to resist that framing. It is not nostalgia. It is about a set of people for whom the digital alternative genuinely does not work, and it is a larger group than the banks' own figures suggest. The closures have accelerated. In my constituency we have lost branch after branch, always with the same letter, always citing declining footfall, and always pointing to the post office as the alternative. The post office network is doing heroic work, but sub-postmasters are being asked to absorb banking services on remuneration that does not reflect the cost, the security risk, or the time.

I would ask the Minister two things. First, whether the access to cash provisions will include a genuine enforcement mechanism, or whether the regulator will merely be asked to monitor. Second, whether the banking hub model will be rolled out at a pace that matches closures rather than trailing years behind them.

Let me go back to the substance, because the numbers matter here and I want them on the record properly. The rules of origin in this agreement are stronger than what preceded them. The regional value content requirement rose from 62.5 per cent to 75 per cent. The core parts requirement, which covers engines, transmissions, bodies and chassis, is also at 75 per cent. And for the first time we have a specific requirement covering aluminum and steel purchases by producers, at 70 per cent. That is a floor that did not exist before.

Now, is it everything the industry asked for? No. The definition question around melt and pour for aluminum was not resolved on the timeline we wanted, and I have been straightforward about that in committee. There is a review, and we will pursue it. But the member's characterization suggests the sector was abandoned, and the sector itself does not say that. The industry associations, the smelters in Quebec, and the unions representing the workers have all supported ratification. I would invite the member to explain why he believes he understands their interests better than they do.

On the labour value content provision, which nobody opposite has mentioned, we secured a requirement that a substantial proportion of vehicle content be produced at a wage floor. That is a genuinely novel instrument in trade agreements, and it addresses the wage arbitrage that hollowed out manufacturing across this continent for a generation.

We negotiated in a difficult environment against a counterparty that was willing to walk away. The result is defensible on its merits.

Recruitment into certain specialties has been hard everywhere, and there are real questions about whether low-volume services deliver the outcomes that higher-volume centres do. What is not legitimate is the pattern we have seen repeatedly: a temporary suspension on safety grounds, followed by a period during which the suspension makes recruitment impossible, followed by a permanent closure justified on the basis that the service has not been operating.

I would ask the Minister for three things. Publication of the clinical review in full. A commitment that no permanent decision will be taken before public consultation. And a recruitment plan with a budget attached.

Let me get to the substance. The core of the problem is that responsibility is distributed across several Departments and agencies in such a way that no one body can be held accountable for the outcome. Each can point, entirely accurately, to the parts of the process that fall outside its remit. The result is a system in which everyone is diligent and nothing works. I have raised individual cases with three different Departments and received three courteous replies, each explaining that the matter is for one of the others.

What is needed is not a new strategy document. We have strategy documents. What is needed is a single accountable office with a budget line, a published implementation plan with dates attached, and a requirement to report to a committee of this House on progress against those dates. Where that model has been applied in other areas it has worked, not because the officials suddenly became more capable, but because someone could be asked a direct question and had to answer it.

I want also to mention the people who have been in touch with me directly, some of whom have been raising this for the better part of a decade. They have been consulted repeatedly. They have contributed to reviews, sat on working groups, and given their time without payment. They are, understandably, running out of patience with a process that appears to substitute consultation for action.

I would ask the Minister to give a commitment on timelines rather than on intentions, and to indicate when the funding allocation will be published.

I raise it because it bears directly on the constitutional question before us. The defence usually offered for hereditary monarchy is that it removes the headship of state from politics and provides continuity without the divisiveness of an election. That defence rests entirely on the assumption that the person who inherits will exercise the residual powers of the Crown with restraint. There is no mechanism to ensure this. There is only the hope that the individual concerned will have been formed by training and temperament into someone who declines to use what is constitutionally available to them.

We were fortunate in the twentieth century. The abdication removed a monarch whose judgment was, on the evidence, extremely poor, and it did so before the war rather than during it. The reign that followed, and the one after it, were models of scrupulous constitutional propriety. But fortune is not a system of government, and building an arrangement that depends on it is a peculiar thing for a country that prides itself on institutional wisdom.

I am not, in this debate, proposing abolition, and I know that the majority in this House and in the country do not favour it. What I am proposing is that we look seriously at codifying the prerogative powers, at removing the remaining discretionary elements around the appointment of a Prime Minister and the granting of a dissolution, and at ending the practice of Queen's consent, whereby legislation touching the Crown's interests is shown to the palace before this House sees it.

Those are modest reforms. They would cost nothing. And they would mean that the next time we are unlucky, it would not matter as much.

Christopher Browning's study of a single reserve police battalion made this point more powerfully than any statistic: ordinary men, given the option to step aside, mostly did not.

The assessment framework we use places heavy weight on incremental cost-effectiveness expressed through a single threshold. For a medicine treating a common condition with a large evidence base, that works reasonably well. There are workable alternatives. Several jurisdictions operate a separate pathway for rare disease medicines with a different set of decision criteria, including managed access arrangements under which a medicine is reimbursed provisionally while real-world outcome data is collected, with reimbursement contingent on the data. Let me remind the House how we got here. There were serious allegations. A committee of this House ordered the production of documents. The order was not complied with. The documents were eventually provided to a body that operates under conditions of secrecy and reports in redacted form, on the argument that national security required it. What is proposed is that documents be produced to a committee of parliamentarians who hold appropriate clearances, with a process for redaction supervised by a former judge, and with the committee itself sitting in camera where necessary. That model has functioned in other Westminster jurisdictions for years. The objection cannot be that it is unsafe; it can only be that it is effective.

We have been very good at announcing investment zones, freeports and enterprise sites. We have been considerably less good at ensuring that the people living within a few miles of them have the qualifications to take the jobs. The fix is not complicated but it is unglamorous. It requires the further education college in the area to be funded to run the specific courses the incoming employers need, on a timescale that begins before construction finishes rather than after. It requires the employers to commit to a number of apprenticeships as a condition of the site agreement, and to have those commitments monitored. And it requires the funding formula for adult education to stop penalising colleges for enrolling people who need to retrain in mid-career, which it currently does through the qualification-level restrictions.

The bill does two principal things. It repeals a number of mandatory minimum penalties, and it expands the availability of conditional sentences. Let me take them in turn.

On mandatory minimums, the evidence is not really in dispute among people who study sentencing. They do not deter, because deterrence depends on the perceived likelihood of being caught rather than on the penalty attached. They transfer discretion from judges, who see the offender and hear the circumstances, to prosecutors, who exercise it through charging decisions that are not subject to review. They produce guilty pleas from innocent people facing an unacceptable risk at trial. And they have been struck down by the courts repeatedly, which means Parliament has been passing provisions that are then litigated at public expense for years before being invalidated.

They have also had a documented and disproportionate effect on indigenous and Black offenders, which is not incidental to the sentencing outcomes but a direct consequence of removing the judicial discretion that Gladue requires courts to exercise.

On conditional sentences, the objection I hear most often is that this will place dangerous people in the community. It will not. A conditional sentence is available only where the sentence imposed is under two years and where the court is satisfied that serving it in the community poses no danger. Those conditions are in the statute and they are applied by judges every day.

I want to make the economic argument rather than simply the moral one, because I think the moral argument, however strong, has already been made and lost once in this Chamber and I would prefer not to repeat the experience.

The debt incurred during this crisis is not comparable to household borrowing, and every serious economist says so. It is long-dated, it is denominated in our own currency, a substantial portion of it is held by the central bank, and the servicing cost as a share of national income is at a historically low level. The constraint is not the stock of debt but the cost of servicing it relative to growth. If growth exceeds the effective interest rate, the ratio falls without any fiscal consolidation whatsoever. That is not a heterodox position; it is the arithmetic that the fiscal authorities themselves use.

So the question is what supports growth. And the answer, on the evidence of the last decade, is not a contraction in public investment. We ran that experiment. Public investment was cut sharply, productivity growth flatlined for the longest period in modern record, and the debt ratio was not reduced as promised because the denominator stopped growing. Whatever else one says about that period, it did not achieve its own stated objective.

What I fear is that the political economy will override the analysis, as it did before. There will be a narrative about living beyond our means. There will be a search for categories of people who can be described as not contributing. And the cuts will fall on local government, on social security and on capital budgets, because those are the ones that can be cut quickly.

We should say now that we will not accept it.

Instead, what we have is a department that treats each mode as a separate policy silo with a separate advisory body, and a supply chain office that was announced with some fanfare and has produced, as far as I can determine, one report.

Let me describe the problem concretely. A container arrives at the Port of Vancouver. Whether it moves promptly depends on rail capacity, on chassis availability, on trucking labour, on the customs release, on warehouse space in the interior, and on whether the highway or rail corridor through the mountains is open, which in recent years has been an open question for weeks at a time. Each of those is regulated or influenced by a different body, several of them provincial, and no single entity has visibility across the whole chain, let alone authority over it.

When the atmospheric river events severed both the rail lines and the highways in 2021, that lack of visibility became a national emergency. Nobody could say with confidence what was in transit, what was perishable, what was critical, or what should be prioritized when partial capacity was restored. The decisions that were made were made well, by people improvising, but they were improvised.

So my recommendation is not merely mapping for its own sake. It is a single national supply chain data platform, with mandatory reporting from the major nodes, held by the federal government, accessible to shippers and to provinces, and used to identify chokepoints before they fail rather than after.

The second recommendation is on resilience investment. The national trade corridors fund is oversubscribed by a wide margin, and the projects it does not fund are not thereby unnecessary. We are choosing, implicitly, to accept a level of fragility, and we should make that choice explicitly with the costs stated.

Annual allocations that lapse at year end force communities to spend in the fourth quarter, at the worst prices, on the shortest timelines, in the most difficult season for construction in the north. The resilience point is the one I want to develop, because it is the structural failure underneath the immediate crisis. For decades we have been told that comparative advantage means we should specialize in extracting and shipping raw materials and buy everything else. When prices are high, that produces revenue that governments spend, and when prices crash, as they always do, the same governments discover that they have no other tax base and no other employer. We have been through this cycle in the eighties, in the late nineties, in 2015, and now again, and each time we resolve to diversify and each time the resolution lasts until prices recover.

Diversification is not achieved by announcing it. It requires processing capacity here rather than shipping unrefined product elsewhere for the value to be added. It requires a manufacturing policy, which we have not had in any meaningful sense since the auto pact. It requires investment in the research capacity of universities that is stable rather than subject to reallocation every budget cycle. And it requires treating the workers in the resource sector as assets to be redeployed rather than as a problem to be managed, which means training funded before the layoffs rather than after.

We have all watched it operate. The technique is to pose the question, to note that it has not been satisfactorily answered, and then to treat the absence of an answer as evidence. Where an answer is given, the response is that the answer came from an official source and is therefore suspect. The structure is unfalsifiable by design, and the people who deploy it know that, which is why the tone is always one of wounded reasonableness.

What makes it dangerous rather than merely tiresome is the second stage. The questions are never random. They cluster. They concern the same small set of groups, in every country where this rhetoric appears, and the answer implied by the question is always the same answer. It has been the same answer for a very long time and the questioners are aware of the lineage even when they deny it, because the vocabulary is borrowed intact from earlier periods and it has not been updated because it does not need to be.

The hon. Lady is right that this is not confined to one part of the political spectrum, and I think that is the most important thing said in this debate. We are all comfortable identifying it when it comes from our opponents. The test of seriousness is whether we identify it when it comes from people whose views we otherwise share, and on that test the record of every party in this House, including mine, is imperfect.

The answer is not to refuse to engage. It is to name the technique, describe what it is doing, and decline to accept its framing.
